content:
Aang invited me to dinner by saying, “We should talk about something,” which was a cruel thing to do to anyone with an imagination.

For the rest of the day I pictured every possible disaster.

The council had rejected our housing proposal.

Someone had died.

Toph had discovered a new category of crime.

Katara hated me.

Aang wanted me to stop coming around.

By the time I reached their house, I had emotionally survived several tragedies that had not happened.

Toph opened the door.

“You’re loud tonight.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Exactly.”

She stepped aside.

The dining room smelled like roasted vegetables, sesame oil, and something sweet. Aang stood at the stove with an apron tied badly over his robes. Katara was slicing scallions. Four bowls sat on the table.

Four.

My stomach tightened.

Aang looked over his shoulder. “Hi.”

“Hi.”

Katara smiled. “You look terrified.”

“Your boyfriend said we should talk.”

Aang winced. “I said it like that?”

“Yes.”

Toph shut the door behind me. “I told him it sounded like a breakup.”

“We’re not even—” I stopped.

Toph grinned.

Katara pointed the knife at Aang. “This is why I told you to invite them normally.”

“I thought being direct was better.”

“Direct would have been ‘come to dinner.’”

Aang put down the spoon. “I’m sorry.”

I laughed because the alternative was screaming.

“Can we eat before whatever this is?”

“Yes,” all three said.

That did not help.

Dinner began normally enough.

Aang had made vegetable dumplings. Katara had made soup. Toph had apparently contributed by buying alcohol and insulting the shopkeeper until he gave her a better bottle.

We talked about work.

Toph’s students had bent a gate into the shape of a turtle-duck.

Katara had convinced the clinic board to train more nonbender medics instead of relying entirely on healers.

Aang had spent three hours mediating an argument about flags.

“What was wrong with the flags?” I asked.

“Everything, according to everyone.”

“Did you solve it?”

“No. I suggested no flags.”

Toph choked on her drink.

Katara covered her face.

“What?” Aang said. “It was fair.”

“It was very Air Nomad of you,” I said.

“Thank you.”

“That was not a compliment.”

“I’m keeping it.”

The ease of the meal almost made me forget the conversation waiting underneath it.

Then Katara set down her spoon.

“Aang told us about the survey trip.”

I looked at Aang.

He immediately lifted both hands. “Not details that were private.”

“What details were private?” Toph asked.

Aang ignored her.

Katara’s gaze stayed on me. “He told us he likes you.”

I could hear my heartbeat in my ears.

Toph said, “We knew.”

“Thank you, Toph.”

“You’re welcome.”

Katara continued. “I like you too.”

There are sentences that arrive gently and still rearrange a room.

That was one.

My eyes dropped to the table.

Four bowls.

Four pairs of hands.

Aang’s fingers curled around his cup. Katara’s rested flat beside hers. Toph leaned back, but both feet were planted on the floor.

“You don’t have to say anything yet,” Katara said.

“That sounds suspiciously reasonable.”

“I am capable of being reasonable.”

Toph snorted.

Katara kicked her under the table.

Toph kicked back.

Aang caught his bowl before the table shook enough to spill it.

I laughed, and the pressure in my chest loosened.

“What about Toph?” I asked.

Silence.

Toph’s expression changed.

For once, I had managed to surprise her.

“What about me?”

I met her unseeing gaze.

“You’ve made it very clear you know how I react to you.”

Aang made a tiny delighted sound.

Katara elbowed him.

Toph’s mouth twisted. “Yeah.”

“Do you react to me?”

Her eyebrows rose.

I had never seen Toph Beifong speechless.

It was magnificent.

“Your heartbeat just changed,” I said.

Katara laughed so suddenly she had to put down her cup.

Aang bent over the table.

Toph pointed at me. “That was dirty.”

“You taught me.”

“I’m so proud.”

Then her grin faded into something smaller.

“Yeah,” she said. “I do.”

The truth sat among us.

It did not solve anything.

It made solving things possible.

Aang rubbed the back of his neck. “There’s another part.”

“Of course there is.”

He glanced at Katara, then Toph.

Katara reached for his hand.

Toph’s fingers tapped once against the table.

Aang said, “This isn’t only about you joining Katara and me.”

I waited.

“We’ve been…” He searched for a word.

“Idiots,” Toph offered.

Katara sighed. “Complicated.”

“Cowards,” Toph corrected.

Aang laughed nervously. “There have been feelings for a while.”

“Between all of you?”

Katara’s thumb moved across Aang’s knuckles.

“Not all in the same way,” she said. “Aang and I have been together for years. That’s real. It’s not changing.”

“I wouldn’t want it to.”

Relief passed through her face.

She continued. “Toph and I… we’ve always been close. Sometimes close in ways neither of us wanted to name.”

Toph’s jaw shifted.

Katara looked at her. “You can tell me I’m wrong.”

Toph’s reply was immediate. “You’re not.”

Aang looked down at the table. “And Toph and I…”

“Have been annoying each other since childhood,” I said.

Toph grinned. “Romantically, apparently.”

Aang laughed.

Then he became serious again.

“We don’t want you to be the excuse we use to avoid talking about that.”

That was the sentence that made me trust the conversation.

Not because it made everything simple.

Because it refused to make me responsible for their unfinished business.

I leaned back in my chair.

“What do you actually want?”

Aang answered first. “I want to keep loving Katara.”

Katara’s hand tightened around his.

“I want to find out what this is with you.”

He glanced at Toph.

“And I want to stop pretending I don’t love Toph in a way that might be more than friendship.”

Toph looked deeply offended by being discussed sincerely.

Katara said, “I want the same. But I don’t want a relationship where everyone has to feel exactly the same thing at exactly the same time.”

“Good,” Toph said. “Because that sounds fake.”

“What do you want?” I asked her.

Toph was quiet longer than either of them had been.

“Choices,” she said finally. “My own. Yours. Theirs. I want nobody deciding that because we’re together, I have to move in, get married, have kids, share a toothbrush, or start talking about feelings before breakfast.”

“I support the toothbrush boundary,” I said.

Aang nodded solemnly. “Very important.”

Katara laughed.

Toph’s shoulders loosened.

Then all three looked at me.

I understood why Aang’s invitation had frightened me.

It was easier to imagine rejection than to imagine being wanted in a way that required an answer.

“I don’t know what I want long-term,” I admitted.

“That’s allowed,” Katara said.

“I know I care about all three of you.”

Toph’s foot shifted under the table until it touched mine.

“I know I’m attracted to all three of you.”

Aang tried not to smile too brightly and failed.

“I know I don’t want to be somebody’s experiment.”

“You won’t be,” Katara said.

“And I don’t want to be added to a relationship like another chair.”

Toph tapped the table. “Good. Chairs are boring.”

I laughed.

Aang reached one hand across the table, palm up.

Not grabbing.

Offering.

After a moment, Katara put her hand over his.

Toph put hers beside Katara’s, not on top, because apparently even symbolic gestures needed structural independence.

I looked at the three of them.

Then I put my hand into the mess.

Four hands.

Four bowls.

No promise beyond honesty.

It should have felt small.

Instead it felt like the first plank laid across a river.

Something we could cross only if we kept building it together.

We tested our new rules the same night.

Toph stole food from my bowl.

“That was mine.”

“Shared household resources.”

“We do not share a household.”

“Preparing early.”

Katara pointed her chopsticks at her. “Ask.”

Toph froze with the dumpling halfway to her mouth.

The table became very quiet.

It was absurd. We had discussed jealousy, privacy, public scrutiny, travel, danger, and the possibility that some relationships among us might grow faster than others. Yet here we were, caught on a dumpling.

Toph slowly lowered it.

“Can I have this?”

“No.”

Aang nearly choked laughing.

Toph turned toward me in outrage. “You made me ask just to say no?”

“I wanted it.”

“You monster.”

Katara covered her mouth, shoulders shaking.

I ate the dumpling while maintaining eye contact with Toph, which was pointless in every conventional sense and somehow still felt like winning.

A minute later I slid the last scallion pancake toward her.

“I don’t want charity.”

“It’s not charity. I hate scallions.”

Toph accepted this immediately.

Aang looked around the table with the soft, startled expression he wore when happiness caught him off guard.

“What?” Katara asked.

“Nothing.”

“That means something.”

He rubbed the back of his neck. “I just like this.”

Toph chewed. “The part where nobody lets me eat?”

“The part where we can say no and still be here afterward.”

That quieted us.

Katara reached for his hand.

I thought about bridges again—not one dramatic span, but boards laid down one at a time. Ask. Answer. Stay.

Toph broke the mood by stealing Aang’s dessert.

He had not yet learned to guard it.
